la:verb:aspicio.gloss: to look at, towards, or upon; behold, gaze at or upon; view, see, examine, survey, inspect, investigate; regard, respect, admire, look to.
senses: to look at, towards, or upon; behold, gaze at or upon; view, see, examine, survey, inspect, investigate; regard, respect, admire, look to.

la:verb:aspicio.html:
a-spĭcĭo (adsp-, Jan; asp-, others except Halm, who uses both), spexi, spectum, 3, v. a. (aspexit = aspexerit, ),
to look to or upon a person or thing, to behold, look at, see.
Lit., constr. in the ante - class. per. sometimes with ad; but afterwards with the acc., with a finite clause, or absol.; in eccl. Lat., with in with acc., and super with acc.
With ad: aspice ad me,: aspicient ad me,: aspicere ad terram,: ad caelum,: Aspice nunc ad sinisteram, (Ritschl, spice): ad Scrofam,; cf. the epitaph of Pacuvius: Adulescens, tametsi properas, te hoc saxum rogat, Ut se[se] aspicias, etc., ap. —(β With acc.: Aspice hoc sublimen candens, Enn. ap. : templum Cereris, id. ap. : me, Pac. ap. : aspicite (me) religatum asperis Vinctumque saxis, Att. ap. ; : me huc aspice,: faciem alicujus,.—In Plaut. twice with contra: aspiciam aliquem

contra oculis, Cas. 5, 3, 2: Th. Aspicedum contra me. Tr. Aspexi. Th. Vides? Tr. Video, Most. 5, 1, 56; so, non audebat aspicere contra Deum,: formam alicujus aspicere,: tergum alicujus,: aspicite ipsum: contuemini os, etc.,: me,: sic obstupuerant, sic terram intuebantur, sic furtim non numquam inter se aspiciebant, etc.,; so : aspicis me iratus,: hominis omnino aspiciendi potestatem eripere,: ut nemo eorum forum aut publicum aspicere vellet,: aliquid rectis oculis,: Aspicit hanc torvis (oculis),: aspiciunt oculis Superi mortalia justis,: aliquid oculis aequis,: aspice vultus Ecce meos,: horrendae aspectu,: aspice nos hoc tantum,look on us thus much only, Wagner: Aspice Felicem sibi non tibi, Romule, Sullam, poët. ap. .—In pass. (rare): unde aliqua pars aspici potest,: pulvis procul et arma adspiciebantur,; : super triginta milia armatorum aspiciebantur,; ; ; : Septentrionem ibi adnotatum primā tantum parte noctis adspici,: quasi eum aspici nefas esset,; ; : adspici humana exta nefas habetur,.—

Absol.: Vide amabo, si non, quom aspicias, os inpudens videtur,: postquam aspexi, ilico Cognovi,.—
With in with acc.: in terram aspicere,; : in caelum,.—(ε) With super with acc.: super castra aspicere,—
Transf.
Of things in space, to look toward, lie toward: tabulatum aspiciat meridiem,: cryptoporticus non aspicere vineas, sed tangere videtur,: ea pars Britanniae, quae Hiberniam aspicit,: terra umidior quā Gallias, ventosior quā Noricum aspicit,.—
Of persons: nobilissimi totius Britanniae eoque in ipsis penetralibus siti nec servientium litora aspicientes,.—
With the access. idea of purpose (cf.: adeo, aggredior, etc.), to look upon something in order to consider or examine it; and in gen. to consider, survey, inspect (freq. in Liv.): hujus ut aspicerent opus admirabile,: Boeotiam atque Euboeam aspicere jussi,: in Boeotiā aspiciendae res,: Ap. Claudium legatum ad eas res aspiciendas componendasque senatus misit,; ; —
Trop.
In gen.: sic in oratione Crassi divitias atque ornamenta ejus ingenii per quaedam involucra perspexi; sed ea cum contemplari cuperem, vix aspiciendi potestas fuit,: sic evolavit oratio, ut ejus vim atque incitationem aspexerim, vestigia ingressumque vix viderim,observed, noticed,: in auctorem fidei,: in remunerationem,.—So esp., to examine, reflect upon, to consider, weigh, ponder (most freq. in the imperat.: aspice, see, ponder, consider, etc.).
With acc.: Postea [tu] aspicito meum, quando ego tuum inspectavero,: neque tanta (est) in rebus obscuritas, ut eas non penitus vir ingenio cernat, si modo (eas) aspexerit,attends to them,: aspice, ait, Perseu, nostrae primordia gentis, Ov M. 5, 190.—
With a finite clause.
In the subj.: qui semel aspexit, quantum dimissa petitis Praestent, etc.,has weighed, considered,: aspiciebant, quomodo turba jactaret aes etc.,: aspiciebant, ubi (Jesus) poneretur,: Quin tu illam aspice, ut placide adcubat,: quin aspice, quantum Aggrediare nefas,: Aspice, venturo laetentur ut omnia saeclo!: Aspice, Plautus Quo pacto partes tutetur amantis ephebi, ut patris attenti ... Quantus sit dossennus, sqq.: Aspice, num mage sit nostrum penetrabile telum,: aspice, si quid loquamur,: Aspice, qui coeant populi,: Qualem commendes, etiam atque etiam aspice,: aspice, Quanto cum fastu, quanto molimine circumspectemus etc., .—
In the indic. (rare): Aspice, ut antrum Silvestris raris sparsit labrusca racemis,: Aspice, ut insignis spoliis Marcellus opimis Ingreditur,: quantas ostentant, aspice, vires,: Aspice, quem gloria extulerat,: aspicite, quae fecit nobiscum,.—Also, to take into consideration, to have in view: si genus aspicitur, Saturnum prima parentem Feci,.—
Esp.
To look upon with respect, admiration: erat in classe Chabrias privatus, sed eum magis milites quam qui praeerant, aspiciebant,.—
Aliquem, to look one boldly in the face, to meet his glance: Lacedaemonii, quos nemo Boeotiorum ausus fuit aspicere in acie, (cf. supra, I., the passage from ). —
Lumen aspicere, to see the light for to live: odi celebritatem, fugio homines, lucem aspicere vix possum,; ; cf. the foll. number fin.—
Ad inchoative (as in addubito, addormio, aduro, etc.), to get a sight of, to see, perceive, descry: perii, si me aspexerit,: forte unam aspicio adulescentulam,; : respexit et equum alacrem laetus aspexit,; so : tum vero Phaëthon cunctis e partibus orbem Aspicit accensum,; : aspicit hanc visamque vocat,; 2, 714; 3, 69; 3, 356; 3, 486; 7, 384; 7, 791 et saep.: Quem simul aspexit scabrum intonsumque,.—Hence trop.: lumen aspicere, to see the light for to be born: ut propter quos hanc suavissimam lucem aspexerit, eos indignissime luce privārit,; cf. supra, II. B. 3.

la:adj:asper.html:
asper, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. (aspra = aspera, Enn. ap. , but Vahl. ad reads
spissa instead of aspra: aspris = asperis,; aspro = aspero,) [etym. dub.; Doed. foll. by Hinter connects it with ἀσπαίρω, to struggle, to resist; Corssen, Ausspr. II. p. 593, regards asper (i. e. ab spe) as the proper opposite of prosper (i. e. pro spe); thus asper originally meant hopeless, desperate; v. also II. p. 870; cf. the use of res asperae as the opposite of res prosperae]; as affecting the sense of touch, rough, uneven (opp. lēvis or lenis; syn.: scaber, acutus, insuavis, acerbus, amarus, mordax, durus).
Lit.: lingua aspera tactu,; cf. ; ; : mixta aspera levibus,: in locis (spectatur) plani an montuosi, leves an asperi,: Quid judicant sensus? dulce, amarum; lene, asperum,: tumulus asperi (sc. saxibus) soli,: saxa, Enn. ap. ; ; Pac. ap. Mar. Vict. p. 2522 P.; Att. ap. ; ; ; cf. Leucas,: loca,, and : viae asperae,: vallis aspera, et saep.: unda, Enn. ap. : glacies,: hiems,; Claud. ap. Prob. Cons. 270: Phasis, i. e. frozen, ice-bound, Prob. ap. ; and of climate: aspera caelo Germania,harsh, severe,: arteria. the windpipe (v. arteria), ; .—Of raised work (i. e. bas-relief, etc., as being rough), as in Gr. τραχύς (cf. exaspero): aspera signis Pocula,: Cymbiaque argento perfecta atque aspera signis,: signis exstantibus asper Antiquus crater, (cf.: stantem extra pocula caprum,): Summus inaurato crater erat asper acantho,: aspera pocula,: ebur,: balteus,: cingula bacis,; cf. Drak. ad : nummus,not worn smooth, new,; cf. : mare,agitated by a storm, rough, tempestuous,.—Of things that have a rough, thorny, prickly exterior: barba,: sentes,: rubus,: mucro, (cf. : pugionem vetustate obtusum asperari saxo jussit; v. aspero).—
Meton., of food: He. Asper meus victus sanest. Er. Sentisne essitas? He. My fare is very rough. Er. Do you feed on brambles? ; cf. ; also of a cough producing hoarseness: quas (fauces) aspera vexat Assidue tussis,.—
Subst.: aspĕrum, i, n., an uneven, rough place: latens in asperis radix,: aspera maris,: propter aspera et confragosa,: per aspera et devia,: erunt aspera in vias planas,; .—Also in the sup. absol.: asperrimo hiemis Ticinum usque progressus,.—
Transf.
Of taste, rough, harsh, sour, bitter, brackish, acrid, pungent: asperum, Pater, hoc (vinum) est: aliud lenius, sodes, vide,: asper sapor maris,: allium asperi saporis; quo plures nuclei fuere, hoc est asperius,: asperrimum piper,: acetum quam asperrimum,.—
Of sound, rough, harsh, grating, etc.: (pronuntiationis genus) lene, asperum,.—Hence a poet. epithet of the letter R (also called littera canina), .—In rhetoric, rough, rugged, irregular: quidam praefractam et asperam compositionem probant; virilem putant et fortem, quae aurem inaequalitate percutiat,; cf. : duram potius atque asperam compositionem malim esse quam effeminatam et enervem,. And in gram., spiritus asper, the h sound, the aspirate, P.—
Of smell, sharp, pungent: herba odoris asperi,.—
Trop.
Of moral qualities, rough, harsh, hard, violent, unkind, rude (cf.: acerbus, acer, and Wagner ad ): quos naturā putes asperos atque omnibus iniquos,: orator truculentus, asper, maledicus,: aspera Juno,: juvenis monitoribus asper,: patres vestros, asperrimos illos ad condicionem pacis,; cf. : rebus non asper egenis,: cladibus asper,exasperated,: asperaque est illi difficilisque Venus,unfriendly,; cf. : (Galatea) acrior igni, Asperior tribulis, fetā truculentior ursā,: Quam aspera est nimium sapientia indoctis hominibus,: asper contemptor divom Mezentius,: aspera Pholoe,coy,.—Of a harsh, austere, rigid view of life, or manner of living: accessit istuc doctrina (sc. Stoicorum) non moderata nec mitis, sed paulo asperior et durior quam aut veritas aut natura patiatur,: (Stoici) horridiores evadunt, asperiores, duriores et oratione et verbis, (v. asperitas, II. A.): (Cato) asperi animi et linguae acerbae et immodice liberae fuit, sed rigidae innocentiae,: (Karthago) studiis asperrima belli,, ubi v. Wagner: Camilla aspera,; cf.: gens laboribus et bellis asperrima,: virgo aspera,i. e. Diana,.—
Of animals, wild, savage, fierce: (anguis) asper siti atque exterritus aestu,: bos aspera cornu, i. e. minax,; cf. : ille (lupus) asper Saevit,: lupus dulcedine sanguinis asper,: ille (leo) asper retro redit,: tigris aspera,; : (equus) asper frena pati,.—
Of things, rough, harsh, troublesome, adverse, calamitous, cruel, etc. (most freq. in the poets): in periculis et asperis temporibus,: qui labores, pericula, dubias atque asperas res facile toleraverant, : mala res, spes multo asperior, (our) circumstances are bad, (our) prospects still worse, : venatus,: bellum,; : pugna,; : fata,: odia,.—Absol.: multa aspera,; —Of discourse, severe, abusive: asperioribus facetiis perstringere aliquem,; : verba,; ; : vox,.—Adv.
Old form asperĭter, roughly, harshly: cubare, Naev. ap. ; Plaut. ap. P.—
Class. form aspĕrē (in fig. signif.), roughly, harshly, severely, vehemently, etc.
Transf.: loqui,; : dicere,: syllabae aspere coëuntes,.—
Trop.: aspere accipere aliquid,: aspere et acerbe accusare aliquem,: aspere agere aliquid,: aspere et ferociter et libere dicta,; : aspere et vehementer loqui,: ne quid aspere loquaris, * .— Comp.: asperius loqui aliquid,: asperius scribere de aliquo,.—Sup.: asperrime loqui in aliquem,: asperrime pati aliquid,: asperrime saevire in aliquem,.

la:verb:ascribo.gloss: to state in writing, to add in writing
senses: to state in writing, to add in writing
to appoint, to enroll, to enfranchise, to reckon, to number
la:verb:ascribo.html:
a-scrībo (ads-, Baiter, Halm, Weissenb., K. and H.; as-, Kayser), psi, ptum, 3, v. a.,
to annex by writing, to add to a writing (syn.: annumero, addo, insero, attribuo, tribuo).
In gen.
Lit., constr. absol. or with dat., in with acc. or abl.
Absol.: non solum illud perscribunt, quod tum prohibiti sunt, sed etiam causam ascribunt cur etc.,: illud minime auguris, quod adscripsit, ob eam causam, etc.,.—
With dat.: Terentia salutem tibi plurimam adscribit,: coheredem sibi libertum ejus adscriptum,.—
With in with acc. or abl.: hoc tibi respondeo: ascripsisse eundem Sullam in eandem legem: si quid, etc.: nam nisi esset, hoc in omnibus legibus non ascriberetur, (B. and K., in eādem lege): antiquior dies in tuis adscripta litteris,: in alterā epistulā diem non adscribis,do not add the date,: nomen suum in albo profitentium citharoedorum jussit adscribi,; —Esp. freq. of superscriptions and inscriptions: Recita epistulam. TIMARCHIDES VERRIS ACCENSVS APRONIO. Jam hoc quidem non reprehendo, quod ascribit ACCENSVS,: non credo ascripturum esse magno,: novo si marmori adscripserunt Praxitelem suo,: tumulo publice exstructo adscripserant, pro libertate eos occubuisse,: ut qui statuarum titulis pronepotem se Q. Catuli Capitolini semper adscripserit,; ; .—
Trop.
To impute, ascribe, attribute to one the cause of something: hoc incommodum Scipioni ascribendum videtur,: panaces diis inventoribus adscriptum,; ; and (per hypallagen, cf. Rudd. II. p. 393): cur autem ascribimus illum his lacrimis (instead of illi has lacrimas),; cf. : nomini meo adscribatur victoria,.—
To place to one's credit, i. e. to settle, fix, designate, appoint: eidem (servo) adscripsisse legatum,bequeathed to him,.—Poet.: culpam lues, olim cum adscriptus venerit poenae dies,.—
Adscribere sibi aliquid, to apply, refer something to one's self: qui facere quae non possunt, verbis elevant, Adscribere hoc debebunt exemplum sibi,.—
Esp., t. t., to enroll, enter in a list (as citizen, soldier, colonist, etc.): ascribi se in eam civitatem voluit,to be entered, received as a citizen,: si qui foederatis civitatibus ascripti fuissent,: urbanae militiae adscribebatur,: adscribantur ex Judaeis in exercitu regis ad triginta milia virorum,: adscripti dicebantur qui in colonias nomina dedissent, ut essent coloni, Paul. ex Müll.: colonos Venusiam adscripserunt,; so ; ; ; 35, 9 al.: coloniam deduxit adscriptis veteranis,; so also of ambassadors,.—
Trop.
To reckon or number in a class, include among: adscripsit Liber Satyris poëtas, (cf. : scribe tui gregis hunc): aliquem ordinibus deorum,: nationes Germanis an Sarmatis adscribam, dubito,: aliquem antiquis temporibus,.—
To add or join to: ad hoc genus ascribamus etiam narrationes apologorum,: admiratus eorum fidem tyrannus petivit, ut se ad amicitiam tertium adscriberent,; so ; : tu vero ascribe me in talem numerum,: suae alicujus sententiam,: unus A. Gabinius belli maritimi Cn. Pompeio socius ascribitur, i. e. additur,—Hence also of attributes of a deity: Jovi aquila adscribitur,is ascribed,.

la:verb:aspernor.html:
aspernor (wrongly ads-), ātus, 1,
v. dep. a. [for ab-spernor, as as-pello for abpello, as-porto for ab-porto; cf. ab init.; Doed. Syn. II. p. 179, and Vanicek, p. 1182], lit., to cast off a person or thing (ab se spernari; cf. sperno and spernor); hence, to disdain, spurn, reject, despise (simply with the accessory idea of aversion = recuso, respuo, reicio, and opp. to appeto, concupisco; on the other hand, contemnere, not to fear, is opp. to metuere, timere; and despicere, not to value a thing, is opp. to revereri; cf. Doed. Syn. cited supra; class.; very freq. in Cic.; more rare in the poets): alicujus familiam, (aspernari = recusare, avertere, non agnoscere, Don.).
Lit.: gustatus id, quod valde dulce est, aspernatur,: nemo bonus ... qui vos non oculis fugiat, auribus respuat, animo aspernetur,; so : regem ut externum aspernari,: matrem,: de pace legatos haud aspernatus,: hanc (proscriptionem) nisi hoc judicio a vobis reicitis et aspernamini,: voluptatem appetit, ut bonum: aspernatur dolorem, ut malum,; so, ut quodam ab hospite conditum oleum pro viridi adpositum, aspernantibus ceteris, solum etiam largius appetisse scribat,: si voluptatem aspernari ratione et sapientiā non possemus,: querimonias alicujus aspernari, contemnere ac neglegere,: regis liberalitatem,; : diis aspernantibus placamina irae,: deditionem alicujus,; et saep.: consilia,: sententiam,: honorem,: militiam,: disciplinam,: virtutem,: panem,: imperium, et saep.: Interea cave sis nos aspernata sepultos,: aspernabantur ceteros, * : haud aspernanda precare,; .—With inf. as object: illa refert vultu non aspernata rogari,: dare aspernabantur,. —In Cic. once, to turn away, avert (not from one's self, but from something pertaining to one's self): furorem alicujus atque crudelitatem a suis aris atque templis, Clu. 68 fin.—
Trop.: qui colore ipso patriam aspernaris,deny,.—!*? Pass.: qui habet, ultro appetitur; qui est pauper, aspernatur, is held in contempt, ap. P.: regem ab omnibus aspernari, Auct. B. Afr. 93: aspernata potio,.—Hence, aspernanter, adv. (qs. from the part. aspernans, which does not occur), with contempt, contemptuously: aliquid accipere,; so .— Comp., .—Sup. prob. not used.

as, assis, m. (nom. assis, Don. ad , and Schol. ad ; old form assārĭus, ii, m.; and in the
gen. plur. assariūm, Müll.; P.) [εἷς, Dor. αἴς, Tarent. ἄς, Hinter].
In gen., unity, a unit; as a standard for different coins, weight, measure, etc. (in Rode, perfectus numerus, the perfect number, fundamental number), acc. to the duodecimal system, divided into 12 parts, or uncias, with the following particular designations: uncia = 1s./12 duodecima (sc. pars) sextans = 2/12 = 1s./6 sexta quadrans = 3/12 = 1s./4 quarta, also teruncius or triuncis triens = 4/12 = 1s./3 tertia or quincunx = 5s./12 sextans cum quadrante semissis s. semis = 6/12 = 1s./2 dimidia septunx = 7s./12 quadrans cum triente bessis s. bes = 8/12 = 2/3, for beis s. binae partes assis. dodrans = 9/12 = 3s./4 terni quadrantes dextans s. decunx = 10/12 = 5s./6 quini sextantes deunx = 11s./12 undecim unciaeThe uncia was again divided into smaller parts: semuncia = 1/2 uncia = 1/24 assis. duella = 1/3 uncia = 1/36 assis. sicilicus (-um) = 1/4 uncia = 1/48 assis. sextula = 1/6 uncia = 1/72 assis. drachma = 1/8 uncia = 1/96 assis. hemisecla = 1/12 uncia = 1/144 assis. scripulum = 1/24 uncia = 1/288 assis.The multiples of the as received the following designations: dupondius = 2 asses. tripondius s. tressis = 3 asses. (quadressis) = 4 asses. quinquessis = 5 asses. sexis (only in the connection decussissexis in . c.) = 6 asses. septissis = 7 asses. octussis = 8 asses. nonussis (novissis?) = 9 asses. decussis = 10 asses. bicessis = 20 asses. tricessis = 30 asses, and so on to centussis = 100 asses. (Cf. Müll.)
Esp.
As a copper coin, the as was, acc. to the ancient custom of weighing money, originally a pound (asses librales or aes grave), of the value of about 8 8d./89, or 16 2/3 cents, and was uncoined (aes rude) until Servius Tullius stamped it with the figures of animals (hence pecunia, from pecus); cf. ; sqq. In the first Punic war, on account of the scarcity of money, the as was reduced to a sixth part of its original weight, i. e. two ounces; hence asses sextantarii (of the value of about 1 103d./297, or 2.8 cents), and the state gained five sixths. In the second Punic war, and the dictatorship of Fabius, the as was again reduced one half, to one ounce; hence asses unciales, about equal to 200d./297, or 1.4 cents. Finally, the Lex Papiria (A.U.C. 563, B.C. 191) reduced the as to half an ounce; hence asses semiunciales = 100d./297, or 7.9 1/3 mills, which continued as a standard even under the emperors. In all these reductions, however, the names of coins remained, independent of the weight of the as: uncia, sextans, quadrans, etc.; cf. Grotef. Gr. II. p. 253 sq.—From the small value of the as after the last reduction, the following phrases arose: quod non opus est, asse carum est, Cato ap. : Quod (sc. pondus auri) si comminuas, vilem redigatur ad assem,: viatica ad assem Perdiderat,to the last farthing,: ad assem impendium reddere,: rumores Omnes unius aestimemus assis,: Non assis facis?.—Hence,
The proverbs,
Assem habeas, assem valeas, your worth is estimated by your possessions, : crumena plena assium,.—
Assem elephanto dare, to give something (as a petition, and the like) with trembling to a superior (a metaphor derived from trained elephants, which, after playing their parts, were accustomed to take pay for themselves, which was given them with fear by the multitude; cf. ), Augustus ap. , and ; Varr. ap. —
In inheritances and other money matters, where a division was made, the as, with its parts, was used to designate the portions. Thus haeres ex asse, sole heir; haeres ex semisse, he who receives one half of the inheritance; haeres ex dodrante, he who receives three fourths; and so, haeres ex besse, triente, quadrante, sextante, etc.; ex semiunciā, ex sextulā, ex duabus sextulis, etc.,; ; ; et saep.: Nerva constituit, ut tu ex triente socius esses, ego ex besse,: bessem fundi emere ab aliquo,: quadrans et semissis fundi,; hence, in assem, in asse, or ex asse,in all, entirely, completely,: vendere fundum in assem,; so and 9: in asse,: sic in asse flunt octo menses et dies decem,: ex asse aut ex parte possidere,; ; ; —
As a measure of extent.
An acre, acc. to the same divisions as above, from scripulum to the as, : proscindere semissem, iterare assem,.—
A foot, .—
Of weight, a pound, acc. to the same division; cf. Fann. Pond. 41: In haec solide sexta face assis eat,.→ Mathematicians (v. Vitr. l. c.) called the number 6 perfectus numerus (since 1 + 2 + 3 = 6), and formed, accordingly, the following terminology: 1 = sextans, as a dice-number . unio. 2 = triens . . . . . . . . . . binio. 3 = semissis . . . . . . . . . . ternio. 4 = bessis (διμοιρος) . . . . . quaternio. 5 = quintarius . . . . . . . quinio. 6 = perfectus numerus . . . . senio. 7 = ἔφεκτος, sex adjecto asse = 6 + 1. 8 = adtertiarius, sex adjectā tertiā = 6 + 2 (ἐπίτριτος). 9 = sesquialter, sex adjectā dimidiā = 6 + 3 (ἡμιόλιος). 10 = bes alter, sex duabus partibus additis = 6 + 4 (ἐπιδίμοιρος). 11 = adquintarius, sex quinque partibus additis = 6 + 5 (ἐπιπεντάμοιρος). 12 = duplio (διπλασίων).

a-stringo (ads-, Ritschl, Baiter, Halm, Jahn, Keil; as-, Fleck., Merk., Kayser), inxi, ictum, 3, v. a.,
to draw close, to draw, bind, or tie together, to bind, to tighten, contract (syn.: constringo, stringo, alligo, obligo, vincio).
Lit.: (hunc) adstringite ad columnam fortiter,: ad statuam astrictus est,: manus,: vinculorum, id est aptissimum ... quod ex se atque de iis, quae adstringit quam maxume, unum efficit,: astringit vincula motu,: laqueos,: artius atque hederā procera adstringitur ilex,is twined around with ivy,: adstringi funibus,: aliquem adstringere loris,: pavidum in jus Cervice adstrictā dominum trahat,with a halter round his neck, (Jahn, obstrictā): aspice ... Quam non adstricto percurrat pulpita socco, not drawn close, loose;poet. for a negligent style of writing, : Ipse rotam adstringit multo sufflamine consul,checks,: balteus haud fluxos gemmis adstrinxit amictus,: frontem,to contract, knit,; : labra porriguntur et scinduntur et adstringuntur,: frondem ferro,to cut off, clip,; so, alvum, to make costive (opp. solvere, q. v.), ; .—Of the contraction produced by cold: nivibus quoque molle rotatis astringi corpus,; so ; : ventis glacies astricta pependit,: Sic stat iners Scythicas adstringens Bosporus undas,: vis frigoris (corpora) ita adstringebat,; .—Hence, also, to make colder, to cool, refresh: ex quo (puteo) possis rursus adstringere,: corpus astringes brevi Salone, Mart. 1, 49, 11 (acc. to Varr. in a pass. sense in the perf., adstrinxi for adstrictus sum, Fragm. ap. ).—Of colors, to deaden: ita permixtis viribus alterum altero excitatur aut adstringitur, (diff. from alligare, which precedes; v. alligo, I. B.).—Also of an astringent, harsh taste: radix gustu adstringit,.—
Trop., to draw together, draw closer, circumscribe; to bind, put under obligation, oblige, necessitate: ubi adfinitatem inter nos nostram adstrinxeris,: vellem, suscepisses juvenem regendum; pater enim nimis indulgens, quicquid ego adstrinxi, relaxat,; so, mores disciplinae severitate, Spald.: ad adstringendam fidem,: hac lege tibi meam astringo fidem,: quo (jure jurando) se cuncti astrinxerant,: hujus tanti officii servitutem astringebam testimonio sempiterno,to confirm, secure, Wund.: religione devinctum astrictumque,: disciplina astricta legibus,; : lege et quaestione,: suis condicionibus,: auditor nullā ejus modi adstrictus necessitate,: orationem numeris astringere, et saep.: adstringi sacris,to be bound to maintain,: inops regio, quae parsimoniā astringeret milites,: ad temperantiam,: ad servitutem juris,: illa servitus ad certa se verba adstringendi,: milites ad certam stipendiorum formulam,; : me astringam verbis in sacra jura tuis,; : magno scelere se astringeret,; ; so ; perh. also ; instead of this abl. of class. Latin, we sometimes find in comedy apparently the gen.: et ipsum sese et illum furti adstringeret,made guilty of, charged himself with,: Homo furti sese adstringet, (cf.: Audin tu? hic furti se adligat,; Draeger, Hist. Synt. I. § 209, regards this as a vulgar extension of the use of the gen. with verbs of accusing, convicting, etc., but Klotz, s. v. astringo, regards it as really an old dative, furtoi furti; cf. quoi cui).—Of reasoning or discourse, to compress, abridge, bring into short compass: Stoici breviter adstringere solent argumenta, (cf. : Haec sic dicuntur a Stoicis, concludunturque contortius); : premere tumentia, luxuriantia adstringere, Frotsch., Halm.—Hence, astrictus (ads-), a, um, P. a., drawn together, tight, narrow, close.
Lit.: limen astrictum,shut,: alvus fusior aut astrictior,: corpus astrictum, i. e. alvus dura,: genus morbi astrictum,costiveness,: gustu adstricto,of a harsh, astringent taste,.—

Transf., to furnish with a rough, wounding exterior (cf. 1. asper, I.): sagittas inopiā ferri ossibus asperant,to point,.—Hence, also, to whet, to sharpen: pugionem vetustate obtusum asperari saxo jussit,: abruptaque saxa asperat, (cf. : nisi cautibus asper Exarsit mucro, and exaspero).—

la:noun:aspectus.html:
aspectus (adsp-), ūs, m. (
gen. aspecti, Att. ap ; cf. P.; Rudd. I. p. 103, n. 46; dat. sing. aspectu, like jussu, manu, etc., ; cf. Schneid Gr II. 332) [aspicio].
Act., a seeing, looking at, a look, sight.
Absol.: intellegens dicendi existimator uno aspectu et praeteriens de oratore saepe judicat, Cic : e quibus (litteris tuis) primo aspectu voluptatem cepi, quod erant a te ipso scriptae, hic primo aspectu inanimum quiddam se putat cernere, : urbs situ est praeclaro ad aspectum,: voci tamen et aspectui pepercit, et saep.—
With gen. of obj. or adj. for gen.: carere aspectu civium,: hominum aspectum lucemque vitare,: aspectum civium gravari,: se aspectu alicujus subtrahere,: ab aspectu alicujus auferri,: aspectum alicujus fugere, Sen Hippol. 734: aspectum alicujus rei exuere,: si te aspectus detinet urbis,: in aspectu earum,: violare sacra aspectu virili, i. e. virorum,. in aspectu tuo gaudebit, .—In plur.: sic orsus Apollo Mortales medio aspectus sermone reliquit, i. e. mortalium,.—
Physically, the sight, glance: lubricos oculos fecit (natura) et mobiles, ut aspectum, quo vellent, facile converterent,: si contendemus per continuationem, acri aspectu utemur, Auct. ad .—
The sense of sight: Sed mihi ne utiquam cor consentit cum oculorum aspectu, Enn. ap. ' quicquid sub aspectum oculorum cadit, : caelum ita aptum est. ut sub aspectum et tactum cadat,: aspectum omnino amittere,: res caecae et ab aspectūs judicio remotae,.—
Pass. (i. e. transferred to the object seen).
The visibility, appearance: adspectu siderum,: In sedecim partes caelum in eo adspectu divisere Tusci,, where Jan reads spectu.—
The manner of appearance, appearance, look, aspect, presence, mien, countenance.
In gen.: quadrupes aspectu truci, Pac. ap. : Horribili super aspectu mortalibus instans,: erat rotis horribilis aspectus,: pomorum

jucundus aspectus, ; : erat aspectus ejus sicut fulgur,: aspectus faciei illius immutatus est super Sidrach etc.,: fuit (Iphicrates) et animo magno et corpore imperatoriāque formā, ut ipso aspectu cuivis iniceret admirationem sui,: Canidia et Sagana horrendae aspectu,: apes horridae adspectu,: (rex) erat terribilis aspectu,: lignum (erat) aspectu delectabile,: Bucephalus adspectu torvo,: Oceanus cruento aspectu,—Hence,

Of shape, the form, appearance: herba adspectu roris marini,; : super similitudinem throni similitudo quasi aspectus hominis,: quasi aspectus equorum, ib. Joel, 2, 4.—
Of color, the color, appearance, look: carbunculi adspectūs nigrioris,: discolor,: Cum color albus in cute fuerit et capillorum mutaverit aspectum,; ; .

astus, ūs, m.
Curtius suggests the Sanscr. aksh = to reach, hit, and ὀξύς, swift; and Vanicek, ascia and ἀξίνη, with the idea of sharpness; others ἀσκέω, to practise

Rib.: Nisi ut astu ingenium linguā laudem et dictis lactem lenibus, p. 189: nam doli non doli sunt, nisi astu colas,: Sed ut astu sum adgressus ad eas!; ; ; : astu providere,: astu rem tractare,: Consilio versare dolos ingressus et astu, Incipit haec,: ille astu subit,: aliquem astu adgredi, : astus belli,: libertae,: oratio, quae astu caret, pondero modo et inpulsu proeliatur,.—In plur.: astus hostium in perniciem ipsis vertebat,: praeveniens inimicorum astus,; 12, 45; : Ulixes nectit pectore astus callidos,: nunc advoca astus, anime, nunc fraudes, dolos,: ad insidiarum astus,.

la:verb:assumo.html:
as-sūmo (ads-, Lachm., Halm, B. and K., Weissenb., K. and H.; ass-, Merk.), mpsi, mptum, 3, v. a.,
to take to or with one's self, to take up, receive, adopt, accept, take.
In gen.
Lit.: Plura sibi adsumunt quam de se corpora mittunt,: cibus atque umor membris adsumitur intus,; so of nourishment,; , n. 17; : numquam committet, ut id, quod alteri detraxerit, sibi adsumat,: sacra Cereris adsumpta de Graeciā,: socius et administer omnium consiliorum adsumitur Scaurus,: eos in societatem consilii avunculi adsumunt,: adulescentes conscii adsumpti,: in societatem armorum,; so, in consilium,; : in consortium,: nec decet aliter filium adsumi, si adsumatur a principe,i. e. is adopted,; 8, 3: uxorem,: si rursum (uxor) adsumeretur,: adsumptis duobus filiis ire perrexit,; : Tunc adsumpsit eum Diabolus,: adsumit Jesus Petrum,: quem (arietem) adsumens obtulit holocaustum pro filio,; et saep.: in familiam nomenque, et saepe: cautum dignos adsumere, to take or choose as friends only those worthy of you, : adsumpsit Jesus duodecim, i. e. as his disciples,. —So of the assumption of our Lord to heaven: Dominus Jesus adsumptus est in caelum, ; .—
Trop.: libero tempore, omnis voluptas adsumenda est, omnis dolor repellendus,: laudem sibi ex aliquā re,: ut acer equus pugnae adsumit amorem,: omne quod sumatur in oratione, aut ex suā sumi vi atque naturā aut adsumi foris,: alii (loci) adsumuntur extrinsecus,; Wund.: orator tractationem orationis sibi adsumet,.—Also, like arrogare, to usurp, to claim, assume, arrogate: neque mihi quicquam assumpsi neque hodie adsumo,; Auct. ad : cogam Assumptumque patrem commentaque sacra fateri,.—Of discourse, to take up, begin (eccl. Lat., after the Hebrew): At ille adsumptā parabolā suā ait,; ; ib. Job, 27, 1; 29, 1.—
Esp.,
Sometimes, like accipio, without the idea of action, to receive, obtain: fetus Melliferarum apium sine membris corpora nasci, Et serosque pedes serasque assumere pennas,: Qui sperant in Domino, adsument pennas sicut aquilae,: a ventis alimenta adsumere,: illas assumere robora gentes,.—
To take in addition to, to add to: si quis aliam quoque artem sibi adsumpserit,; : aliquantum jam etiam noctis adsumo,: ne qui postea adsumerentur,: Butram tibi Septiciumque et Sabinum adsumam,.—
In logic, t. t., to add or join to a syllogism the minor proposition: Ea (propositio vera ac perspicua) est hujus modi: Si quo die Romae ista caedes facta est, ego Athenis eo die fui, in caede interesse non potui. Hoc quia perspicue verum est, nihil attinet approbari; quā re adsumi statim oportet hoc modo: fui autem Athenis eo die, ; ; .—
In gram.: adsumpta verba.
Epithets, ἐπίθετα, . —

la:verb:aspiro.html:
a-spīro (adsp-, Baiter, Rib., Merk., K. and H.; asp-, Kayser, Halm, Müller), āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
Neutr.
To breathe or blow upon; constr. with ad, the dat., or absol.: ad quae (granaria) nulla aura umida ex propinquis locis adspiret,: ut ne ad eum frigus adspiret,: pulmones se contrahunt adspirantes,exhaling,: Lenius aspirans aură,: amaracus illum Floribus et dulci adspirans complectitur umbrā,: adspirant aurae in noctem, rise at or toward night, : si minuma adspirat aura,: tibia adspirat choro,accompanies,—
Trop.: alicui, to be favorable to, to favor, assist (the figure taken from a fair breeze): aspira mihi,: quibus aspirabat Amor,: adspirat primo fortuna labori,: adspirate canenti,: di, coeptis adspirate meis,.—Also absol.: magno se praedicat auxilio fuisse, quia paululum in rebus difficillimis aspiravit, Auct. ad (cf. afflo).—
To aspire to a person or thing, to desire to reach or obtain, i. e. to approach, come near (esp. with the access. idea of striving to attain to); constr. with ad, in with acc., the dat., a local adv., or absol. (class.; freq. in Cic.): qui prope ad ostium adspiraverint, Lucil. ap. : quid enim quisquam ad meam pecuniam me invito aspirat? quid accedit?; so : tu ad eum Ciceronem numquam aspirasti,; so : omnes aditus tuos interclusi, ut ad me adspirare non posses,: aspirare in curiam,: in campum,: ne non modo intrare, verum etiam adspicere aut aspirare possim,; : nec equis adspirat Achillis,: sed non incendia Colchis adspirare sinit,.— Trop.: sed haec ad eam laudem, quam volumus, aspirare non possunt,arrive at, attain to,: bellicā laude aspirare ad Africanum nemo potest,: haec etiam in equuleum coniciuntur, quo vita non adspirat beata,; .—
In gram., to give the h sound, to aspirate (cf. aspiratio, II. B.): consonantibus,: Graeci aspirare solent,; Nigid. ap. .—
Act.
To breathe or blow upon, to infuse, instil; lit. and trop. (poet. or in post-Aug. prose): Juno ventos adspirat eunti,sends favoring winds,: adspiravit auram quandam salutis fortuna,: dictis divinum amorem,: novam pectoribus fidem,: nobis tantum ingenii aspiret,.— *
To breathe or blow upon; trop. of the sea, to wash: insula adspiratur freto Gallico,is washed,.

la:adj:astutus.html:
astūtus, a, um, adj.
a lengthened form of the ante-class. astus, like versutus from versus, cinctutus from cinctus; and astus itself has the form of a P. a., q. v. init.
,
shrewd, sagacious, expert; or (more freq., cf. astutia) in mal. part., sly, cunning, artful, designing, etc. *
Ante-class. form astus, a, um: asta lingua, Att. ap. .—
Class. form astūtus: malus, callidus, astutus admodum,: Causam dicere adversus astutos, audacīs viros, valentes virgatores,: non tam astutus, neque ita perspicax,: verum ego numquam adeo astutus fui, Quin etc.,: ratio,: nihil astutum,: hoc celandi genus est hominis non aperti, non simplicis, non ingenui; versuti potius, obscuri, astuti, fallacis,: astuti Getae,: Parthorum astutae tela remissa fugae,: ut est astuta et ingeniosa sollertia,, where Jan omits astuta et: gens non astuta, nec callida, et saep.: pro bene sano Ac non incauto fictum astutumque vocamus,: homo sagax et astutus,: Est vir astutus multorum eruditor,: vulpes,: consilium,—As subst. (eccl. Lat.): Astutus omnia agit cum consilio,; .—Comp.: fallacia astutior,: si qui me astutiorem fingit (followed by callidius),: qui custodit increpationes, astutior fiet,.—* Sup.: astutissimus adversarius,: astutissima calliditas, id. Civ. Dei, 21, 6.— Adv.: astūtē, craftily, cunningly: astute comminisci aliquid,: docte atque astute captare,: consulte, docte atque astute cavere,: Astute, shrewdly done, : astute labefactare aliquem,: satis astute adgredi aliquem,: astute reticere aliquid,: astute nihil agere, Matius ap. .— Comp.: astutius ponere aliquid, Müll.—Sup.: astutissime componere aliquid,: astutissime excogitare,: astutissime fingi, , 19, 5.

la:noun:astutia.gloss: cunning, craftiness, cleverness, shrewdness (adeptness at using tricks)

la:noun:astutia.html:
astūtĭa, ae, f.
astutus

(Trag. Lat.; afterwards supplanted by astus, q. v.): est nobis spes in hac astutiā,: nec copiast [Me expediundi], nisi si astutiam aliquam corde machinor, Fleck.; 3, 4, 7; ; : nunc opus est tuā Mihi ad hanc rem expromptā malitiā atque astutiā,; : quod si aut confidens astutia aut callida esset audacia, vix ullo obsisti modo posset,: quae tamen non astutiā quādam, sed aliquā potius sapientiā secutus sum,: qui (Deus) adprehendit sapientes in astutiā eorum,; ; .—Also plur.: in regionem astutiarum mearum te induco,; so : Hem astutias, Don.: aliter leges, aliter philosophi tollunt astutias,; .

to scatter or strew a person or thing with something; splash over

la:verb:aspergo.html:
a-spergo (adsp-, Ritschl, Jan; asp-, others; in MSS. sometimes aspar-go, v. Cort. ad , and Wagner ad , and infra examples from Lucr. and Hor.; cf. 2. aspergo), ersi, ersum, 3, v. a.

Trop.: cum clarissimo viro non nullam laudatione tuā labeculam aspergas,fasten upon,: ne qua ex tuā summā indignitate labes illius dignitati aspersa videatur,: notam alicui, (cf.: allinere notam,).—So of an inheritance, to bestow, bequeath something to, to set apart for: Aebutio sextulam aspergit,.—Poet.: alas: lacteus extentas aspergit circulus alas,.—In gen., to add to, to join, = adjungere: si illius (sc. Catonis majoris) comitatem et facilitatem tuae gravitati severitatique asperseris,: huic generi orationis aspergentur etiam sales,; : hos aspersi, ut scires etc.,—

Lit.: ah, guttulā Pectus ardens mihi adspersisti (cf. supra, aquam),: quas (sedes) nec nubila nimbis Aspergunt,: ne aram sanguine aspergeret,; so ,

33; : sanguine mensas,; and with de: asperget de sanguine ejus (turturis) parietem altaris,: vaccam semine,: Vinxit et aspersas altera vitta comas,the sprinkled hair, (Müller, † acceptas): imbre lutoque Aspersus, K. and H.; : aquā,; : hyssopo,: cinere,: terrā, al.—

Trop.: (Mons Idae) primo parvis urbibus aspersus erat,dotted over with,: aures gemitu,to fill,, ext. 1: auditiunculā quādam aspersus, i. e. imbutus,instructed,: aspersi corda a conscientiā malā,.—Esp., to spot, stain, sully, defile, asperse: hunc tu vitae splendorem maculis aspergis istis?; so also absol.: leviter aspersus,: istius facti non modo suspitione, sed ne infamiā quidem est aspersus,; so : aspergebatur etiam infamiā, quod, etc.,; so : aliquem linguā, Auct. ad : e quibus unus amet quāvis aspargere cunctos, i. e. quibusvis dicteriis perstringere, laedere, K. and H.

Bruti auguris commentandi causā, ut adsolet, venissemus,: legiones, non laetae, ut adsolet, neque insignibus fulgentes,; ; .

la:verb:assequor.gloss: to follow someone in order to come up to him; pursue, go after
senses: to follow someone in order to come up to him; pursue, go after

la:verb:assequor.html:
as-sĕquor (ads-, Fleck., B. and K., Halm), sĕcūtus (or sĕquutus; v. sequor), 3, v. dep.,
to follow one in order to come up to him, to pursue.
In gen. (only ante-class. in the two foll. exs.): ne sequere, adsequere, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Müll.: Adsequere, retine,.—Far more freq.,
Esp., to reach one by pursuing him: sequendo pervenire ad aliquem: nec quicquam sequi, quod adsequi non queas,.—Hence, to overtake, come up with a person or thing (with the idea of active exertion; while consequi designates merely a coming up with, a meeting with a desired object, the attainment of a wish; cf. Doed. Syn. III. p. 147 sq. According to gen. usage, adsequor is found only in prose; but consequor is freq. found in the poets): si es Romae jam me adsequi non potes, sin es in viā, cum eris me adsecutus, coram agemus,;

poët. ap. : Pisonem nuntius adsequitur,.—In the histt. also absol.: ut si viā rectā vestigia sequentes īssent, haud dubie adsecuturi fuerint,: in Bruttios raptim, ne Gracchus adsequeretur, concessit,: nondum adsecutā parte suorum,arrived,; .—

Trop.
To gain, obtain, procure: eosdem honorum gradus adsecuti,: immortalitatem,: omnes magistratus sine repulsā,; so : regnum,: nihil quicquam egregium,; : quā in re nihil aliud adsequeris, nisi ut, etc.,: adsecutas virtute, ne, etc.,.—
To attain to one in any quality, i. e. to come up to, to equal, match; more freq. in regard to the quality itself, to attain to: Sisenna Clitarchum velle imitari videtur: quem si adsequi posset, aliquantum ab optimo tamen abesset,: benevolentiam tuam erga me imitabor, merita non adsequar,; so fin.: qui illorum prudentiam, non dicam adsequi, sed quanta fuerit perspicere possint,: ingenium alicujus aliquā ex parte,: ut longitudo aut plenitudo harum multitudinem alterius adsequatur et exaequet, Auct. ad .—
Transf. to mental objects, to attain to by an effort of the under standing, to comprehend, understand: ut essent, qui cogitationem adsequi possent et voluntatem interpretari,: quibus (ratione et intellegentiā) utimur ad eam rem, ut apertis obscura adsequamur,: ut scribas ad me, quid ipse conjecturā adsequare, A fin.: Quis tot ludibria fortunae ... aut animo adsequi queat aut oratione complecti?; Sex. Caecil. ap. : quid istuc sit, videor ferme adsequi,: visum est et mihi adsecuto omnia a principio diligenter ex ordine tibi scribere,: adsecutus es meam doctrinam,; .!*? Pass. acc. to P., but without an example; in , instead of the earlier reading, it is better to read, ut haec diligentia nihil eorum investigare, nihil adsequi potuerit; cf. Zumpt ad h. l., and Gronov. Observ. 1, 12, 107; so also B. and K.

la:verb:assentior.gloss: to agree with; assent to, approve, give assent or approval
senses: to agree with; assent to, approve, give assent or approval
la:verb:assentior.html:
as-sentĭor (ads-, Fleck., B. and K., Halm, Weissenb.; ass-, Merk.), sensus, 4, v. dep.
sentio
(the
act. form assentio, īre, was out of use even in the time of Varro, Fragm. ap. ; cf. Spald. ad . The middle use of the word corresponds far better with its signif. than the active; for while adsentio prop. signif. only sentiendo accedere ad aliquem or aliquid, to make known one's inclination or feeling toward any object, whether in favor of or against it; the middle, assentior, = sentiendo se applicare, designates a friendly joining of one's self to any one. The act. form, adsentio, is found in ; ; Att. and Pompon. ap. ; ; in Cic. only three times in epist. style (which is worthy of notice; cf. absque), Fam. 5, 2, 9; ; and ad Q. Fr. 2, 1, 2; cf. P.; but after the time of the poets of the Aug. per. it is often found, particularly in the post-Aug. histt., together with the class. mid. form, used in like manner: assensit precibus Rhamnusia justis,; ; : cum de aliis rebus adsentire se veteribus Gabinis diceret,: Adsensere atque etc.,; ; ; ; ; ), lit., to join one in opinion, to agree with; hence, to assent to, give assent, to approve, give approval; with dat. or absol.: adsensus sum homini, Lucil. ap. : Adsentio,: adsensi sunt omnes,: cum saepissime tibi senatus maximis sit de rebus adsensus,; : si ulli rei sapiens adsentietur,: cui (sententiae) sunt adsensi ad unum,: quibus (verbis) adsensi sunt in conspectu meo,; : in quibus adsentior sollicitam et periculosam justitiam non esse sapientis, Fragm. ap. P.: sapientem, si adsensurus esset, etiam opinaturum, etc.,: verbo adsentiri,: omnes adsensi sunt partibus dividundis,; : cui non adsentior, Spald.: ne adsentiri necesse esset, et saep.—So of conduct, to yield: quam ob rem adsentire nobis,.— With neutr. acc. aliquid, cetera, etc.: non habeo autem quid tibi adsentiar,: vitiosum est adsentiri quidquam falsum,: cetera adsentior Crasso,: Mihi quoque adsunt testes, qui illut quod ego dicam adsentiant,: illud quod a te dictum est, valde tibi adsentior,; so .!*? Pass.: is (sapiens) multa sequitur probabilia, non comprehensa neque percepta neque adsensa, sed similia veri, nor assented to as perceived by sense (cf. assensio and assensus), .—And impers.: Bibulo adsensum est,.

assensus (ads-), ūs, m.

Poet., an echo: Et vox adsensu nemorum ingeminata remugit,: Aereaque adsensu conspirant cornua rauco,; .

la:verb:assurgo.html:
as-surgo (ads-, B. and K., Rib., Merk., Halm, Weissenb.; ass-, Roth), surrexi, surrectum, 3, v. n.,
to rise up, rise, stand up (cf. ad, II. B.; class.; freq. in Verg., once in Ov., never in Hor.; syn.: surgo, consurgo, insurgo, orior).
Lit.
Of persons: quae dum laudatio recitatur, vos quaeso, qui eam detulistis, adsurgite,: fratrem adsurrexisse ex morbo,: Valentem e gravi corporis morbo adsurgentem, : intortis adsurgens arduus undis,: desine viso adsurgere pulvere,.—Hence, with dat. or absol., to rise up to one, to rise up, out of respect.
With dat.: an quisquam in curiam venienti adsurrexit?: Utque viro Phoebi chorus adsurrexerit omnis,: Ruricolae Cereri teneroque adsurgite Baccho, * : honori numinis,: cum palam esset ipsum quoque iisdem et assurgere et decedere viā,: cum conaretur assurgere,: non adsurrexisse sibi,; so with coram (eccl. Lat.): coram te adsurgere nequeo,.—
Absol.: neque assurgere neque salutare se dignantem,; : et senes adsurgentes stabant,. —In pass. impers.: ut majoribus natu adsurgatur,: cum adsurrectum ei non esset,: ludos ineunti semper adsurgi etiam ab senatu in more est,; : so in a zeugma: haec enim ipsa sunt honorabilia ... salutari, appeti, decedi, adsurgi, deduci, etc. (decedi and adsurgi being impers. here, the other verbs pers.), .—Hence, trop., to give the preference to, to yield to: sunt et Aminaeae vites ... Tmolius adsurgit quibus,yields the palm,.—Poet.: jamque adsurgentis dextrā plagamque ferentis Aeneae subiit mucronem, i.e. dextram attollentis,.—
Of inanimate things: colles adsurgunt,rise,; so , and : Pyramis adsurgit trecentis sexaginta tribus pedibus,: Delos adsurgit Cynthio monte,.—
Transf.
To mount up, to rise, to increase in size, swell, tower up (poet.): cum subito adsurgens fluctu nimbosus Orion,. 535: adsurgens nox aurea,: tumores oriuntur, deinde desinunt, deinde rursus adsurgunt,: non coeptae adsurgunt turres,: terra jacet aggeribus niveis informis septemque adsurgit in ulnas,rises seven ells high,: Adsurgit ceu forte minor sub matre virente Laurus, 244.—
Of mental objects.
To rise: nunc sera querellis Haud justis adsurgis,i. e. break out in complaints,: adsurgunt irae,: in ultionem adsurgere,.—
To rise in courage, to rise (cf. the opp. affligi): gaudet in adversis animoque adsurgit Adrastus,.—
Of style, etc., to rise, soar: raro adsurgit Hesiodus,: neque comoedia cothurnis adsurgit,; cf.: sublimitate heroici carminis animus adsurgat,.

In gen.: medici adsiduitas,constant attendance,: cotidiana amicorum adsiduitas et frequentia,: eorum, qui abs te defensi sunt,: eandemque adsiduitatem tibi se praebuisse postridie,the same unceasing attendance,: summā adsiduitate cotidianā aliquem tractare,.—So of the constant attendance, in the assemblies, of candidates for office (cf.: habitare in oculis,): altera pars petitionis, quae in populari ratione versatur, desiderat nomenclationem, blanditiam, adsiduitatem, etc.,: adsiduitatis et operarum harum cotidianarum putat esse consulatum,: valuit adsiduitate, valuit observandis amicis, valuit liberalitate,: homo aut frugalitatis existimatione praeclara aut, id quod levissimum est, adsiduitate,. —First in Suet., without access. idea, for constant presence, .—

Lit.: saxorum asperitates,: asperitas viarum,: locorum,: angustiae locorumque asperitas,; ; : linguae,: ventris,: squamarum,: faucium,: animi asperitas seu potius animae,hoarseness,: ob asperitatem hiemis,roughness, severity,: asperitas frigorum abest,: densaque cedit Frigoris asperitas,: asperitas luti,dryness, barrenness of the clay,.—Of raised work (cf. 1. asper, I., and exaspero): vasa anaglypta in asperitatemque excisa,with figures in basrelief,.—

Of hearing, roughness, harshness of tone: vocis,: soni,.—

a-scisco (adsc-, Lachm., Baiter, Dietsch, Weissenb., K. and H., Halm in Tac.; asc-, Merk., Kayser, Rib., Halm in Nep.), īvi (in ante-class. and class. Lat. never ii), ītum, 3, v. a.
Lit., to take or receive a thing with knowledge (and approbation), to approve, receive as true: cum jussisset populus Romanus aliquid, si id ascivissent socii populi ac Latini, etc.,: quas (leges) Latini voluerunt, asciverunt,, § 21: quibus (scitis) adscitis susceptisque,: tu vero ista ne adsciveris neve fueris commenticiis rebus assensus,: ne labar ad opinionem, et aliquid adsciscam et comprobem incognitum,.—
Of persons, to receive or admit one in some capacity (as citizen, ally, son, etc.): dominos acrīs adsciscunt,; : perficiam ut hunc A. Licinium non modo non segregandum, cum sit civis, a numero civium, verum etiam, si non esset, putetis asciscendum fuisse,; cf. : [aliā (civitate) ascitā], Halm: Numam Pompilium ... regem alienigenam sibi ipse populus adscivit eumque ad regnandum Romam Curibus adscivit,: aliquem patronum,: socios sibi ad id bellum Osismios, etc., adsciscunt,; so : socius adscitus,: aliquem ducem, Auct. B. Alex. 59, 2: qui non asciverit ultro Dardanium Aenean generumque acceperit urbi,: gener inde provecto annis adscitus,; so : ascivit te filium non vitricus, sed princeps,: tribuni centurionesque adsciscebantur,: aliquem successorem, al.—In the histt. also with in (in civitatem, societatem, senatum, nomen, etc.): adsciti simul in civitatem et patres,: simul in civitatem Romanam et in familias patriciorum adscitus,: aliquem in numerum patriciorum,: inter patricios,: Chauci in commilitium adsciti sunt,: aliquem in penates suos,: aliquem in nomen,; : aliquem in bona et nomen,.—
Transf., in gen., to take or receive a person to one's self; of things, to appropriate to one's self, adopt (diff. from adjungere and assumere, by the accessory idea of exertion and mediation, or of personal reflection; cf. Herz. ad ; ).
Of persons: nemo oppressus aere alieno fuit, quem non ad hoc incredibile sceleris foedus asciverit,: exsulibus omnium civitatium ascitis, receptis latronibus, etc.,: eā tempestate plurimos cujusque generis homines adscivisse dicitur,: Veientes re secundā elati voluntarios undique ad spem praedae adsciverunt,; : in conscientiam facinoris pauci adsciti,.—Poet.: asciscere for asciscere se or ascisci, to join or unite one's self to one (cf.. Accingunt omnes operi, ): ascivere tuo comites sub numine divae centum omnes nemorum,.—
Of things: Quae neque terra sibi adscivit nec maxumus aether, which neither the earth appropriates to itself nor etc., : Jovisque numen Mulciberi adscivit manus, Att. ap. : sibi oppidum asciscere,: Ceres et Libera ... quarum sacra populus Romanus a Graecis ascita et accepta tantā religione tuetur, etc.,; so ; Heins., where Merk. reads acciverit (cf. Web. ad ): peregrinos ritus,: Spem si quam ascitis Aetolum habuistis in armis,: opimum quoddam et tamquam adipatae dictionis genus,: nova (verba) adsciscere, * : quod ipsa natura adsciscat et reprobet, (B. and K., sciscat et probet): adsciscere aut probare amicitiam aut justitiam,; : illa, quae prima sunt adscita naturā, (cf. Beier ad ): hanc consuetudinem

lubenter ascivimus, . —

Sibi, like arrogo, to assume or arrogate something to one's self (very rare): eos illius expertes esse prudentiae, quam sibi asciscerent,: eloquentiae laudem uni sibi,; cf. .—*
To order, decree, or approve also or further, = etiam sciscere: alterum (genus sacerdotum) quod interpretetur fatidicorum et vatium ecfata incognita, quae eorum senatus populusque adsciverit,, ubi v. Moser.— ascītus, P. a. (opp. nativus, innatus, insitus), derived, assumed, foreign: in eo nativum quemdam leporem esse, non ascitum, Halm: proles,; genitos esse vos mihi, non ascitos milites credite,: nec petit ascitas dapes,.

senses: to appoint to, assign, distribute, allot, allocate

la:verb:assigno.html:
assigno (ads-, B. and K., Halm, Weissenb., Jahn, K. and H.), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
In gen.
Lit., to mark out or appoint to one, to assign; hence also, to distribute, allot, give by assigning, as t. t. of the division of public lands to the colonists (cf. assignatio; syn.: ascribo, attribuo): uti agrum eis militibus, legioni Martiae et legioni quartae ita darent, adsignarent, ut quibus militibus amplissime dati, adsignati essent,; so ; : qui (triumviri) ad agrum venerant adsignandum,; ; Sic. Fl. p. 18 Goes.—
Transf., to assign something to some one, to confer upon: mihi ex agro tuo tantum adsignes, quantum corpore meo occupari potest,: munus humanum adsignatum a deo, : apparitores a praetore adsignati,: ordines,: quem cuique ordinem adsignari e re publicā esset, eum adsignare,: equum publicum,; so : equiti certus numerus aeris est adsignatus,: aspera bella componunt, agros adsignant, oppida condunt, to assign dwellingplaces to those roaming about (with ref. to I. A.), * : natura avibus caelum adsignavit,appointed, allotted,: de adsignandis libertis,. 1 sq.: adsignavit eam vivam, παρέστησεν, he presented her, —
Trop., to ascribe, attribute, impute to one as a crime, or to reckon as a service (in the last sense not before the Aug. period; in Cic. only in the first signification).
In mal. part.: nec vero id homini tum quisquam, sed tempori adsignandum putavit,: haec si minus apta videntur huic sermoni, Attico adsigna, qui etc.,: ne hoc improbitati et sceleri meo potius quam imprudentiae miseriaeque adsignes,; so ; ; ; Planc. ap. : petit, ne unius amentiam civitati adsignarent,' permixtum vehiculis agmen ac pleraque fortuita fraudi suae adsignantes, ; Nigid. ap. ; and without dat.: me culpam fortunae adsignare, calamitatem crimini dare; me amissionem classis obicere, etc., Zumpt.—
In bon. part.: nos omnia, quae prospera tibi evenere, tuo consilio adsignare; adversa casibus incertis belli et fortunae delegare,: Cypri devictae nulli adsignanda gloria est,: sua fortia facta gloriae principis,: hoc sibi gloriae,: si haec infinitas naturae omnium artifici possit adsignari,: inventionem ejus (molyos) Mercurio adsignat,—
Esp.
With the access. idea of object, design, to commit, consign, give over a thing to one to keep or take care of (rare, mostly post - Aug.): quibus deportanda Romam Regina Juno adsignata erat,' Eumenem adsignari custodibus praecepit, ; ; .—Trop.: bonos juvenes adsignare famae,; so .—
To make a mark upon something, to seal it (post-Aug.): adsigna, Marce, tabellas,: subscribente et adsignante domino,; : cum adsignavero iis fructum hunc, shall have sealed and sent, .—Trop.: verbum in clausulā positum adsignatur auditori et infigitur,is impressed upon,.

la:verb:assuesco.gloss: to get used to, become accustomed with, inure to
la:verb:assuesco.html:
as-sŭesco (ads-, B. and K., Rib., Halm, Weissenb.; ads- and ass-, Merk.), ēvi, ētum, 3 (adsuëtus, four syll., ), v. a.,
to use or accustom one to something, to habituate; or, more freq., v. n., to accustom one's self to, to be wont, to be accustomed to.
In gen.; constr. usu. with abl. or inf.; after the Aug. per. also with ad, in with acc., or dat.
With abl. (a constr. unjustly censured by Wunder, Rhein. Mus. 1829, II. p. 288 sq. The idea of the ad, which would require the acc. or dat. case, is not, as at a later period, prominent in the word, but that of suesco; accordingly, pr., to adopt some custom, to addict or apply one's self to a custom or habit, to become accustomed to something; so that the abl. of specification, as in amore affici, pedibus laborare, etc., only designates more specifically the object which is the subject of that custom; cf. Gron. and Drak. ad ; Kritz. ad ; Rudd. II. p. 137 sq.; Ramsh. p. 427; v. also assuefacio): homines labore adsiduo et cotidiano adsueti,; so, vicinitas non infuscata malevolentiā, non adsueta mendaciis,: gens adsueta multo Venatu nemorum,: Odrysius praedae assuetus amore,: genus pugnae, quo adsuērant, Gron.: adsuetae sanguine et praedā aves,; : adsuetus imperio et inmoderatā licentiā militari,: gentes alterius imperio ac nomine adsuetas,; .—
With inf.: fremitum voce vincere,: votis jam nunc adsuesce vocari,: adsueti muros defendere,: Candida de nigris et de candentibus atra Qui facere adsuērat,; ; ; : adsuetus graecari,: auditor adsuevit jam exigere laetitiam,; ; ; : (polypus) adsuetus exire e mari in lacus,: reliquas (legiones) in hiberna dimittere assuerat,.—
With ad or in with acc.: uri adsuescere ad homines ne parvuli quidem possunt,; Fragm. ap. P.: manus adsuetae ad sceptra,: jam inde a puero in omnia familiaria jura adsuetus,; .—
With dat.: mensae adsuetus erili,: Adsuescent Latio Partha tropaea Jovi,: caritas ipsius soli, cui longo tempore adsuescitur,to which one is accustomed,: ex more, cui adsuerunt,: ut quieti et otio per voluptates adsuescerent,: adsuetus expeditionibus miles,: adsueti juventae Neronis,: quo celerius (libri senatorum) rei publicae assuescerent,: Jurationi non adsuescat os tuum,.—Acc. to a rare constr., (ε) With acc. rei in the Gr. manner, εἴθισμαί τι: ne pueri, ne tanta animis adsuescite bella (for bellis),accustom not your minds to such great wars,: Galli juxta invia ac devia adsueti,: frigora atque inediam caelo solove adsuerunt, Baumst.—(ζ) With gen.: Romanis Gallici tumultūs adsuetis,.—
Esp.: alicui, in mal. part.,.— Hence, assŭētus (ads-), a, um, P. a., accustomed, customary, usual: Tempus et adsuetā ponere in arte juvat,: otium des corpori, adsueta vicis,: adsuetos potare fontes,: adsuetam sibi causam suscipit,.—Hence with a comp. and abl.: longius adsueto lumina nostra vident,: adsueto propior,.
